sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
The authors' own summary of the paper's contribution:

> "We propose that automation can be applied to four broad classes of functions: 1) information acquisition; 2) information analysis; 3) decision and action selection; and 4) action implementation... The human performance consequences of particular types and levels of automation constitute primary evaluative criteria for automation design using our model. Secondary evaluative criteria include automation reliability and the costs of decision/action consequences."

Critically, the model is explicitly not prescriptive at the level of a single system: "appropriate types and levels of automation for different systems can vary widely. Our model does not therefore *prescribe* what should and should not be automated in a particular system." What it offers instead is the evaluative machinery for reaching that decision on a stated, checkable basis.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Not an empirical study. This is a conceptual framework paper, synthesizing roughly two decades of prior empirical human-factors and cognitive-engineering research (the paper cites ~80 sources — laboratory experiments, field studies, incident analyses) into a four-stage model, then demonstrating the model's use with a worked design example (recommended automation levels for a future air-traffic-control system, Fig. 4 in the source). No new experimental data is reported; the contribution is the framework and its application procedure (Fig. 3's iterative flow chart: pick a stage → pick a candidate level → test against primary criteria → test against secondary criteria → repeat).

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- **Explicitly a qualitative model, not a quantitative one.** Section V states this directly: "as a qualitative model our approach is meant to provide a framework for design, not a set of quantitative methods." The authors flag this as a real limitation and point to (then-emerging) computational models as future work, not as something this paper delivers.
- **The authors admit they did not weight the criteria against each other.** Also Section V: "we did not discuss how the relative benefits and costs should be weighed... These are difficult issues to which there are no simple answers." A designer using this model still has to make a judgment call about which cost matters most in a given system.
- **The number of levels is only fully specified for one of the four stages.** The 10-point decision/action scale is borrowed from Sheridan & Verplank (1978); the authors explicitly did not specify a level count for information acquisition/analysis, citing insufficient comparative empirical data at the time of writing.
- **Full automation (their level 10) is flagged by the authors themselves as often practically unreachable**, not just risky: full automation "requires highly reliable error handling capabilities and the ability to deal effectively and quickly with a potentially large number of anomalous situations... This requirement currently strains the ability of most intelligent fault-management systems" (footnote 3).
- No sample size applies (this is a synthesis/framework paper), but its own worked recommendations (e.g., the ATC example) are explicitly stated as an *upper bound*, not a required level — the authors repeat this qualifier twice to prevent the model being read as a fixed rule.
